title: Optimal exploration of new products with heterogeneous priors
short_statement: For assortment-based exploration of new products, characterize the optimal ordering/grouping policy when entrants have heterogeneous priors rather than a common prior.
full_statement: A platform repeatedly offers an assortment $S_t$ of at most $c$ products. Incumbent products have known MNL attraction parameters, while entrant products begin with cold-start attraction parameters and independent prior distributions over their true attraction parameters. If a customer purchases entrant $i$, a review reveals $i$'s true attraction parameter; otherwise no information about that entrant is learned. Rewards are generated by MNL purchase probabilities, and regret is measured relative to the assortment that would be optimal if all attraction parameters were known. Baek, Dinev, and Lykouris solve the homogeneous-prior case, where all entrants have the same prior, and show that the optimal EFA policy pairs entrants with top incumbents and chooses the number of entrants to explore through a threshold rule. The open problem is to characterize the optimal policy when entrants have heterogeneous priors: which entrants should be explored first, when should multiple heterogeneous entrants be grouped, and does there exist an index or low-dimensional priority rule that is provably optimal beyond the two-entrant special case?
background: Platforms constantly decide how much scarce display capacity to allocate to new products whose quality is unknown. The Baek-Dinev-Lykouris model is deliberately parsimonious: incumbents have known qualities, entrants require purchases and reviews to reveal quality, and assortment capacity creates a direct opportunity cost. This is not the same as an MNL bandit with unknown choice parameters, because before a review arrives the current choice model is common knowledge; the uncertainty concerns a future change in the choice model after social learning reveals a product's quality. Their homogeneous-prior result is structural rather than merely algorithmic. It explains why a new product should be paired with strong incumbents despite a lower purchase probability, and why the number of entrants explored simultaneously follows a threshold based on entrant potential. Heterogeneous priors remove the symmetry that makes EFA clean: the platform must rank entrants with different upside probabilities, cold-start attractions, and effects on future assortment value.
open_problem: Characterize the optimal assortment-exploration policy for heterogeneous entrant priors under the MNL social-learning model, or prove an optimal index/priority rule for deciding which entrants to explore and whether to group them.
known_results: Baek, Dinev, and Lykouris show that with one entrant it is optimal to include that entrant with the $c-1$ most attractive incumbents. With multiple homogeneous-prior entrants, they characterize the optimal number of entrants to explore simultaneously and show the threshold depends on entrant potential rather than individual purchase probabilities. They also prove that UCB and Thompson sampling can be arbitrarily suboptimal in opposite directions, and that simple heuristics such as always exploring all entrants or exploring one at a time can fail. For heterogeneous priors, they analyze a class with two entrants, two incumbents, and capacity two: the optimal policy is one of exploring entrant 1 first, entrant 2 first, or both together, and the best choice can depend subtly on prior tails. They explicitly leave open whether there is a prior-based index whose ordering is optimal in the general heterogeneous case.

where_posed.text: Open direction in Baek, Dinev, and Lykouris, 'Optimal Exploration of New Products under Assortment Decisions'.

progress.summary: The homogeneous-prior model is solved by EFA, and a two-entrant heterogeneous special case is characterized. General heterogeneous-prior ordering and grouping remain open.

links.title: Optimal Exploration of New Products under Assortment Decisions

counterexample_rationale: Small heterogeneous-prior instances can refute proposed index, ordering, or threshold rules by exact dynamic programming or symbolic regret comparison.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search over two-, three-, and four-entrant finite-prior instances can map optimal policy regions and discover whether any scalar priority statistic survives.

literature.synthesis: The homogeneous-prior result shows that this is not a generic bandit question: assortment substitution and social learning create a specific exploration externality. The two-entrant heterogeneous analysis is especially useful because it demonstrates why a naive ordering by upside, mean, or UCB-like optimism is insufficient. The remaining problem is to identify whether the messy prior dependence still collapses to an index or threshold in larger instances, or whether optimal policies need genuinely history-dependent grouping. A positive result would give a clean operational rule for marketplace experimentation; a negative result would be equally valuable if it identifies the smallest heterogeneous-prior instance where every scalar-index policy fails.

reviewed.ref: Jackie Baek, Atanas Dinev, and Thodoris Lykouris, 'Optimal Exploration of New Products under Assortment Decisions', arXiv 2026
reviewed.result: Solves the homogeneous-prior entrant model, proves failures of UCB and Thompson sampling, and gives a two-entrant heterogeneous-prior characterization while leaving the general index/order question open.

reviewed.ref: Shipra Agrawal, Vashist Avadhanula, Vineet Goyal, and Assaf Zeevi, 'MNL-Bandit: A Dynamic Learning Approach to Assortment Selection', Operations Research 2019
reviewed.result: Develops a foundational dynamic assortment-learning model under MNL choice, useful as a contrast because the unknown object there is the choice model rather than post-review entrant quality.

reviewed.ref: Rusmevichientong, Shen, and Shmoys, 'Dynamic assortment optimization with a multinomial logit choice model and capacity constraint', Operations Research 2010
reviewed.result: Classical capacity-constrained MNL assortment-learning setting that supplies algorithmic background for the assortment component.

reviewed.ref: Talluri and van Ryzin, 'Revenue management under a general discrete choice model of consumer behavior', Management Science 2004

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Build exact dynamic programs for finite-support priors with two to four entrants and small capacity, then search for monotonicity, exchange arguments, or counterexamples to scalar indices. Try statistics based on prior mean, upside tail, cold-start purchase probability, expected regret reduction, and value of information. A proof may need coupling or majorization arguments; a disproof may give two instances with the same candidate index order but opposite optimal exploration order.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed policy characterization must specify the prior family, cold-start attraction parameters, capacity, horizon/regret convention, and whether learning is noiseless or noisy. If the claim is an index theorem, verify it against the two-entrant heterogeneous examples in Baek-Dinev-Lykouris and against exact dynamic programming on small finite-support priors. A numerical counterexample should include all MNL parameters and enough precision to reproduce the optimal-policy comparison.
